484.hook: one Krishna, a whole arena, and everyone sees someone different
484.carry: the world is real; the mind adds the color
484.howItsDone: Classical Yoga, like Samkhya, is taught as a realist philosophy: the world of nature is real, and practice aims at freeing the mind from the coloring it takes on, not at denying the world. The Bhagavata's arena verse pictures the same idea: one Krishna, seen by each mind in its own way.

segments.voice: Mathura, the day of King Kamsa's wrestling match. The whole city is packed into the arena. Then two young cowherds walk in from the gate: Krishna and his brother Balarama. The Bhagavata Purana stops the story right there and looks at the crowd. To the wrestlers, Krishna is a thunderbolt. To the men, the finest of men. To the women, love itself, walking. To the cowherds, their own boy. To wicked kings, the one who'll punish them. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. And to Kamsa, up on his platform, he is death.
screen: `ONE BOY WALKS INTO THE ARENA.` → `THE WRESTLERS SEE A THUNDERBOLT.` → `HIS PARENTS SEE THEIR CHILD.` → `KAMSA SEES HIS DEATH.`

segments.voice: One Krishna. A whole arena. A different Krishna in every mind. The Bhagavata isn't a philosophy book, but it paints exactly what Patanjali argues in sutra 4.15: vastusamye chittabhedat tayor vibhaktah panthah. The thing being the same, because the minds differ, the two go separate ways. Vastu is the real thing out there; chitta is the mind. Notice what Patanjali doesn't say. He doesn't say Krishna is ten things, or nothing, or only a picture in each head. Krishna is really there, walking in. The difference is in the minds. And 4.17 says how: a thing is known when the mind takes on its color. Picture a clear glass set on red cloth. Many teachers read the arena this way: Kamsa's mind is colored by fear, so he sees death. His parents' minds are colored by love, so they see a child. Hindu schools argued about this for centuries. Some Buddhist philosophers of the time held that objects are built by the mind, and the old commentary on these sutras answers them; later, Advaita Vedanta would speak of the world as maya. Yoga, with its sister school Samkhya, takes a plain stand: the world is real. So the trouble was never the world. It's the coloring: the craving and the dread the mind lays on it. Yoga doesn't ask you to deny the chair or the cup or your brother. It asks you to clean the glass. You've seen the small version. In 2015, one photo of a dress split the internet: blue and black, or white and gold. Two siblings remember the same family dinner as a disaster and a delight. Same dress. Same dinner. Different glass.

Vastu, the real object out there. For Patanjali, the world is real; minds differ in how they are colored by it.

485.title: What lights a person?
485.hook: a king asks a sage what we see by when every light goes out
485.carry: the mind is seen; the self is the light
485.howItsDone: In Yoga and Samkhya teaching, the purusha is the unchanging witness and the mind belongs to nature; Vedanta teachers speak of the atman as the witness, sakshi, and point to the Brihadaranyaka's answer to Janaka: the self is a person's light.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: vastu, the real thing out there. One Krishna walked into Kamsa's arena, and every mind saw him in its own color.
screen: `THE WORLD IS REAL; THE MIND ADDS THE COLOR.`

segments.voice: King Janaka, the king who stayed free inside a palace, has a question for the sage Yajnavalkya, and it sounds almost too simple. What does a person see by? By the sun, says Yajnavalkya. And when the sun has set? By the moon. And when the moon has set too? By firelight. And when the fire goes out? By a voice: in the dark, you walk toward the sound. And when the voice falls silent, Yajnavalkya, what light does a person have then? The sage answers: the self is his light.
screen: `WHAT DOES A PERSON SEE BY?` → `SUN. MOON. FIRE. A VOICE.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM GO OUT?` → `THE SELF IS HIS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: That conversation is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the oldest. Its word for that inner light is atman, the self, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: underneath your thoughts and moods is something that isn't a thought or a mood. It's the light they're seen by. Patanjali, in his own school's language, calls it purusha, the seer, and today's sutras argue for it. Sutra 4.18: the turnings of the mind are always known to their master, because the seer does not change. Always. Every thought, even the ones you'd rather nobody saw. Then 4.19: na tat svabhasam drishyatvat. It is not self-luminous, because it is seen. Like the moon, the mind only seems to shine on its own. It's an object, like a cup or a cloud, only subtler, and things that are seen don't light themselves. Sutra 4.21 closes the door. If one mind were lit by another mind, you'd need a third to light that one, and a fourth, forever. The line has to stop at a seer who isn't a mind at all. The Upanishads and the Yoga Sutras describe that seer differently, and Hindu schools still debate how. But they agree on this much: you are not only what you see in yourself. Hindu teachers often call it the witness, sakshi. So when worry fills the room at two in the morning, notice one small thing. The worry is being seen. It's real, and it's lit by something that isn't worry.

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace, and wait for a thought to come. When it does, don't follow it; just notice, this is known, and the same with a sound, a feeling, a plan for later. You don't have to find the knower; rest in the plain fact that each thing is seen.
Svabhasa, self-luminous — what the mind is not. It is seen, so its light is borrowed, from the purusha, the seer that does not change.

486.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras describe viveka, discernment between the seer and the seen, as the turning point of the path; after it, practice is said to become less a struggle and more a natural leaning toward freedom.

segments.voice: Sri Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, liked to tell this one. A tigress dies giving birth beside a flock of goats, and the cub grows up among them. He eats grass. He bleats. He's sure he's a goat. One day a wild tiger comes, and the grass-eater bleats in terror with the rest. The old tiger catches him and drags him to a pond. Look at your face in the water, he says. It's just like mine. The cub bleats a few more times. Then, slowly, he roars.
screen: `A TIGER RAISED BY GOATS.` → `HE EATS GRASS. HE BLEATS.` → `LOOK AT YOUR FACE IN THE WATER.` → `HE ROARS.`

segments.voice: Ramakrishna told it about the teacher who shows you what you already are. Patanjali names the same turning point in sutra 4.25: visheshadarshina atmabhava-bhavana-vinivrittih. For the one who sees the distinction, the making of a self comes to an end. The distinction is yesterday's: the mind is seen, the seer sees. Atmabhava-bhavana is the habit of building a self out of the mind's material, rehearsing it, feeding it. The cub did that every day: I'm the one who eats grass, I'm the one who bleats. Hindu thought has a plain name for that self-building: the ego. Samkhya calls it ahamkara, the I-maker; Patanjali calls the feeling asmita, taking the instrument of seeing for the seer. One look in the water, and the bleating loses its point. Then 4.26: tada viveka-nimnam kaivalya-pragbharam chittam. Then the mind slopes toward discernment and leans toward freedom. Nimna means low ground, the slope water runs down. Freedom stops being a climb. It's downhill. Patanjali stays honest, though. The very next sutra admits that old impressions still throw up other thoughts. The cub bleated a few more times before he roared. We build selves too: out of grades, followers, being the funny one or the smart one, and we keep rehearsing them. Hindu teaching doesn't ask you to fight that self to the death. It asks you to see what you are, and let the act get quieter.
screen: `THE CUB SEES HIS FACE.` · `THE SELF-MAKING HABIT.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `THE MIND SLOPES TOWARD FREEDOM.` · then, large: `SEE THE SEER, AND THE EGO WINDS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, then let your weight settle into the seat, the way water settles into low ground. As small I-thoughts come by, I should, I'm tired, I wonder, let each one roll downhill and away. Rest in whatever is left when they've passed.
Nimna, low, sloping ground. Seeing the seer and the seen as different, the habit of building a self out of the mind winds down, and the mind slopes toward freedom.

487.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, dharma-megha samadhi is described as the last stage before kaivalya, reached only when the practitioner seeks nothing, not even from the highest discernment.

segments.voice: The man-lion has burst out of the pillar, and the demon king is gone. But Narasimha's rage is so fierce that even the gods are afraid to go near him. So they send a small boy: Prahlada, who never stopped remembering Vishnu. The lion's anger cools. He lays his hand on the child's head and says: ask me for anything. And Prahlada, who came through poison and snakes for this god, says no. A servant who wants rewards from his master, he says, isn't a servant. He's a merchant.
screen: `THE MAN-LION'S RAGE.` → `THEY SEND A SMALL BOY.` → `ASK ME FOR ANYTHING.` → `NO. THAT WOULD BE TRADING.`

segments.voice: That's the Bhagavata Purana, and it sits right beside today's sutra. Sutra 4.29: prasankhyane 'py akusidasya sarvatha vivekakhyater dharmameghah samadhih. For one who takes no interest even in the highest knowledge, from discernment in every way, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma. The money word is kusida: lending at interest. An akusida charges none. Prahlada would understand: no trading with what's holiest. Patanjali's yogi reaches the clearest seeing there is and doesn't try to collect on it. No powers, no status, not even keeping it as a trophy. Earlier, Patanjali warned that the powers are obstacles, and that even an invitation from the gods mustn't stir attachment or pride. This is that refusal carried all the way up. Yoga and bhakti, the path of devotion, are different roads, and they meet right here. When even that last wanting goes, what arrives is dharma-megha. Megha is the heavy monsoon cloud. Commentators read the image two ways: a cloud that rains dharma on everything, or one that rains away the last of karma. Either way it isn't a prize. It's weather. The same name, dharma-megha, appears in Buddhist texts for the last stage of the bodhisattva's path: two neighbors reaching for the same cloud. And today? Many Hindus make vows to God: I'll fast if I pass, I'll walk to the temple if she gets well. That's an honest kind of prayer, kept for generations. Prahlada points past it, to a love that has stopped keeping accounts.
screen: `4.29: THE CLOUD OF DHARMA.` · `AKUSIDA: ONE WHO TAKES NO INTEREST.` · `YOGA AND BHAKTI MEET HERE.` · `MEGHA: THE MONSOON CLOUD.` · then, large: `DHARMA-MEGHA COMES TO ONE WHO WANTS NO RETURN.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, keep no account: don't track how calm you are, or how well this is going. If you catch yourself scoring, smile at the scorekeeper and set the pencil down. If you pray, offer the sit to God and ask for nothing back; if you don't, just breathe the way rain falls, not to get anything back.

The Bhagavata says she was shaken to the core. Then the vision closed, and she pulled her boy into her lap, just her son again.

segments.voice: Nothing was added to Yashoda in that moment. The universe had been there all along. A covering came off. Patanjali's last chapter makes that the fruit of the whole path. Sutra 4.30: tatah klesha-karma-nivrittih. From the cloud of dharma, the afflictions and karma cease. The kleshas are the five from the second chapter: not-seeing, the I-am feeling, clinging to pleasure, pushing away pain, and clinging to life. And Patanjali names the root of them all: avidya, not-seeing. That's a big Hindu idea. The deepest problem isn't that you're bad. It's that you can't see what's really there. Then 4.31: tada sarva-avarana-mala-apetasya jnanasya anantyaj jneyam alpam. Then, because knowledge, free of every covering and impurity, is without limit, what remains to be known is little. Avarana is a covering, like a lid. Mala is grime, the dust on a lamp's glass. Knowledge was never small; it was covered. For Yashoda the lid came back down: the Bhagavata says Krishna veiled it again in a mother's love, so she could go on being his mother. For the yogi of 4.30, it stays off. And jneyam alpam, the knowable is little, isn't a claim to know every fact in the world. It's proportion. Next to a light without limits, everything else looks small. You know the small version: a test, a fight, a fear that filled the whole room, until the room opened onto a bigger sky.

segments.voice: Hold lightly one thing you've been trying hard to figure out, a decision, a person, a worry. Then let your attention widen: the room, the building, the sky over it, the whole spread of the day. Let the question sit inside all that space, smaller than it was, with nothing to solve right now.
Klesha, affliction, rooted in avidya, not-seeing. From the cloud of dharma, the kleshas and karma cease, knowledge is uncovered and without limit, and little remains to be known.

489.title: The dancer who bows out
489.hook: a dancer leaves the stage once she's been seen, and the Yoga Sutras end on one small word
489.carry: kaivalya: the seer resting in itself
489.tomorrow: The question that starts the Ramayana
489.howItsDone: Many students of the Yoga Sutras finish a reading of the text by chanting its last sutra, and teachers describe kaivalya as consciousness abiding in its own nature, no longer identified with the mind.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: klesha. Yashoda saw the universe when the covering came off. Knowledge was covered, never small.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE WAS COVERED, NEVER SMALL.`

segments.voice: Samkhya, Yoga's sister school, tells its whole philosophy as a little drama. There's a watcher, who can see but can't move, and a dancer, who can move but can't see for herself: nature, with all its colors. The two need each other, the old text says, like a lame man riding on a blind man's shoulders through a forest. So the dancer dances: the world, the body, every thought and mood, a whole show for one watcher. And once she knows she has truly been seen, she stops. She bows out, and never shows herself to him again.
screen: `A WATCHER WHO CAN'T MOVE.` → `A DANCER WHO CAN'T SEE.` → `A WHOLE SHOW FOR ONE WATCHER.` → `ONCE SEEN, SHE BOWS OUT.`

segments.voice: Patanjali's last sutras tell the same ending. Sutra 4.32: then, their purpose fulfilled, the gunas finish their sequence of change. The gunas are the three strands of nature, what the mind and the world are woven from. Nature has danced for a reason, Patanjali said back in sutra 2.18: to give the seer experience, and then freedom. Purpose served, the dance stops. Sutra 4.33 adds that change is grasped at the end of a transformation, the way you notice a child has grown when the old shoes don't fit. Then the last thread, 4.34: purushartha-shunyanam gunanam pratiprasavah kaivalyam, svarupa-pratishtha va chiti-shaktir iti. Kaivalya is the gunas returning to their source, with nothing left to do for the seer. Or: the power of consciousness, resting in its own nature. Thus. This is the goal Hindus call moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death. Each school names it its own way; Yoga's name is kaivalya, consciousness no longer mistaken for the dance. And the book closes on iti, thus, the word Sanskrit uses to end a quotation or a whole work. Fifty-nine days ago this block opened on atha, now. All four chapters, from the top. Samadhi Pada: stilling the mind's turnings. Sadhana Pada: the practice and the eight limbs. Vibhuti Pada: the powers, and the warning about them. Kaivalya Pada: the mind seen clearly, and set down. Most days we live inside the show: the feed, the mood, the mind performing. The tradition's last word on it is gentle. The show is real, and you were the one it was danced for.
screen: `THE DANCE HAS A PURPOSE.` · `THE GUNAS' WORK IS DONE.` · `KAIVALYA: YOGA'S NAME FOR MOKSHA.` · `FROM NOW TO THUS.` · then, large: `KAIVALYA: THE SEER RESTING IN ITSELF.`

segments.voice: For this last sit with Patanjali, do less than ever: let the body be held, let the breath happen without you, and let thoughts be the gunas finishing their work. You aren't reaching for anything; you're resting in what was already here. If you pray, you can offer these sixty days to God, in whatever words are your own.
Kaivalya. In the last thread: the gunas gone back to their source, and the power of consciousness resting in its own nature, the goal the whole Yoga Sutras points toward.
screen: `KAIVALYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: kaivalya, the seer resting in itself. The dancer has bowed. Tomorrow, a new story begins in a forest: the Ramayana.

490.title: The question that starts the Ramayana
490.hook: the Ramayana opens with a question: is there anyone like this alive today?
490.carry: Rama: dharma lived in a human life
490.howItsDone: Some Hindus read Valmiki's Ramayana in Sanskrit or in translation, a set number of chapters a day; the Bala Kanda, the first book, opens with Valmiki's question and Narada's answer.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

screen: `KAIVALYA. THE SEER KAIVALYA: THE SEER RESTING IN ITSELFS.`

segments.voice: For the next six months, give or take, we're reading one story, in order, a little each day, like a serial: the Ramayana, as Valmiki tells it, book by book. You may know the outline already: a prince, an exile, a kidnapping, a war, a homecoming. But Valmiki doesn't start with a battle or a birth. He starts in a quiet forest hermitage, with one man asking a visitor a question about a person. Who, today, is good all the way through?
screen: `SIX MONTHS. ONE STORY. IN ORDER.` → `NOT A BATTLE. A HERMITAGE.` → `WHO IS GOOD ALL THE WAY THROUGH?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana's first verse sets the scene. Tapah-svadhyaya-niratam: devoted to discipline and study. That describes Narada, the wandering sage, best of those who know how to speak. The one asking is Valmiki, a hermit himself, and his question is a list. Is there anyone in the world right now who is virtuous, and strong, who knows what's right, who's grateful, truthful, firm in his promises? Someone of good conduct, kind to every living being, learned, capable, good to look at? Someone who has mastered himself and conquered his anger, who shines, who envies no one, and yet whom even the gods fear when he's roused in battle? Tradition counts sixteen qualities in that question. Narada answers honestly: those are many qualities, and hard to find together. But I know one. Born in the line of Ikshvaku, people call him Rama. So the whole epic opens as a question about character, and the story that follows is the evidence. That's why Hindus hold Rama up as dharma lived in a human life: not a rulebook, a person. Later devotion calls him maryada purushottama, the best of men, who keeps within what's right. Now the week, from the top. Krishna walked into Kamsa's arena, and every mind saw him in its own color. A king asked what light is left when every light goes out. A tiger cub saw his face in a pond. Prahlada asked for nothing. Yashoda looked into a little mouth and saw everything. The dancer bowed out. And today, a question in a forest: is anyone like this alive?
screen: `A HERMIT ASKS A WANDERING SAGE.` · `SIXTEEN QUALITIES IN ONE QUESTION.` · `NARADA: I KNOW ONE. RAMA.` · `DHARMA, LIVED IN A PERSON.` · then, large: `TAPAḤSVĀDHYĀYANIRATAM.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've known, living or gone, who had some of Valmiki's list: truthful, kind to every living being, slow to anger, grateful. Not perfect, just good in a way you remember; let their face come, and breathe with one of their qualities resting in your chest. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Narada, the wandering sage who answers Valmiki's question. The Ramayana begins as their conversation about character.
screen: `NARADA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Rama, dharma lived in a human life. Narada knew one. Day four hundred ninety, done.
